hypotheses.title: Higher-Order Return Moment: Conditional Crash Risk Skewness via Tanh Z-Score
hypotheses.economic_rationale: Empirical asset pricing (Harvey & Siddique 2000) establishes that rational investors demand a structural risk premium for bearing negative return skewness (crash risk). Stocks exhibiting high rolling positive skewness possess lottery-like payoff distributions and are systematically bid up by speculative retail participants, resulting in lower expected forward returns. Instead of uniform ranking and linear decay, we apply a cross-sectional z-score mapped through a non-linear hyperbolic tangent (tanh) activation and subindustry neutralization. Universal 100% instrument coverage across TOP3000.
confounders: Sudden single-day corporate spin-offs or large recapitalizations distorting rolling 60-day return distributions
hypotheses.falsification_test: Fails during market regimes where lottery-seeking speculative demand continues unabated without mean-reverting.

hypotheses.title: Idiosyncratic Risk Normalization Dislocation via Winsorized Z-Score
hypotheses.economic_rationale: In the model51 risk framework, unsystematic_risk measures return variance uncorrelated with the market factor SPY. When short-term idiosyncratic variance spikes relative to a company's 1-year baseline, it reflects transient stock-specific panic or headline overreaction. As idiosyncratic uncertainty dissipates, prices mean-revert toward fundamental fair value. We introduce a winsorized cross-sectional z-score architecture capped at 3 standard deviations, fully neutralized across subindustries. Completely virgin dataset with zero portfolio correlation.
confounders: Permanent fundamental business model collapse justifying persistent elevated idiosyncratic risk
hypotheses.falsification_test: Fails if high idiosyncratic variance reflects structural solvency degradation that fails to mean-revert.

hypotheses.title: Analyst Forecast Dispersion & Opinion Divergence Penalty
hypotheses.economic_rationale: Diether, Malloy, and Scherbina (2002) demonstrate that securities with high analyst earnings forecast dispersion (high estimate minus low estimate relative to mean EPS) suffer predictable long-term underperformance. Because short-sale constraints prevent pessimistic investors from expressing views, equity prices reflect disproportionately optimistic forecasts. When consensus dispersion narrows, uncertainty clears and price efficiency is restored. We apply winsorized cross-sectional z-scoring and subindustry neutralization.
confounders: Firms covered by only one or two sell-side analysts where high-low spreads are sparse
hypotheses.falsification_test: Fails if high dispersion reflects genuine positive optionality in early-stage growth companies.
